content: Efforts to improve oral health at a population level are supported by public health initiatives and broad-based measures, which also contribute to achieving universal oral health coverage. Simultaneously, advancements in digital technologies have been increasingly utilized, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, to enhance prevention and patient care in oral health. Emerging issues such as the implementation of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, environmental sustainability, pandemic preparedness and resilience, antimicrobial resistance, and oral health in humanitarian and emergency contexts require coordinated attention from both public and private sectors at the national level. The oral health sector, including research, is expected to capitalize on opportunities in operational research, digital innovation, and emerging public health challenges. Strengthening public health and operational research is essential to inform evidence-based decision-making, policies, and advocacy. This involves setting research priorities, allocating dedicated funding, and enhancing the interface between public health science and policymaking. Digital innovations hold significant potential to expand the reach and scope of oral health promotion, disease prevention, and access to care, particularly for remote and underserved populations. These technologies can aid in the training and supervision of oral health professionals, as well as in monitoring and evaluating oral health interventions. Their use should reduce barriers to access, promote self-care, ensure inclusivity, and adhere to ethical standards, including patient confidentiality and privacy. Addressing emerging issues such as pandemic preparedness, antimicrobial resistance, environmental sustainability, and the phase-down of dental amalgam under the Minamata Convention is critical for strengthening the oral health sector. Environmental protection and sustainability in oral health care are vital contributions to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The Minamata Convention aims to reduce the environmental impact of oral health care through measures such as phasing out dental amalgam. Ensuring continuity of essential oral health services during pandemics requires robust planning and preparation. Antimicrobial resistance remains a significant challenge, and oral health professionals play a key role in mitigating this issue through prudent antibiotic prescribing and infection control measures. Additionally, the resilience of oral health services in the face of natural disasters, war, or migration must be considered. The implementation of the Action Plan for Oral Health in South-East Asia (2022–2030) necessitates leadership and collective efforts from health ministries, particularly in countries with less developed oral health policies and systems. A functioning national oral health coordinating entity is essential to lead and coordinate efforts among stakeholders and ensure a multisectoral response. Core elements of a national oral health program include policy leadership, service delivery, workforce development, infrastructure, health promotion, surveillance, research, and partnerships with civil society. The World Health Organization (WHO) will provide leadership and technical support to promote and monitor the Action Plan for Oral Health in South-East Asia (2022–2030). WHO will collaborate with United Nations agencies, WHO collaborating centers, and other partners to strengthen national responses to the oral disease burden through capacity-building. Additional technical documents and guidance will be developed to align with evolving regional and global policies, including the Global Oral Health Action Plan (2023–2030). WHO will also facilitate knowledge exchange and collaboration among Member States to ensure universal access to oral health. Comprehensive and regular monitoring and reporting on the implementation progress of the Action Plan for Oral Health in South-East Asia (2022–2030) will ensure transparency, inform planning and resource allocation, and motivate stakeholder engagement. WHO’s Global Strategy on Oral Health emphasizes the importance of improving oral health surveillance, data collection, and monitoring to inform decision-making and advocacy. This includes standardizing methods for gathering epidemiological data, integrating electronic dental and medical records, and strengthening surveillance of oral diseases. Tracking progress toward 2030 goals for both the Global Strategy on Oral Health and the regional Action Plan is crucial. Strengthening information systems and aligning indicators are key actions to improve monitoring and reporting capacities. Oral health interventions should address the most common population needs, including health promotion, disease prevention, screening, diagnosis, emergency management, and treatment of oral and dental diseases. These actions include counseling on oral hygiene, nutrition, and tobacco cessation, as well as promoting self-examination and behavior change to reduce sugar intake. Screening for oral diseases, oral cancer, and developmental anomalies, as well as managing oral infections and trauma, are critical components. Treatment options include fluoride varnish application, restorative procedures, scaling, root planing, and prosthetic fabrication. Ensuring access to these services is essential for improving oral health outcomes.
